title: Brutus
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi039.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: phalereus enim successit eis senibus adulescens eruditissimus ille quidem horum omnium, sed non tam armis institutus quam palaestra. Itaque delectabat magis Atheniensis quam inflammabat. Proces serat enim in solem et pulverem, non ut e militari tabernaculo, sed ut e Theophrasti doctissimi hominis umbraculis.
passages.english: For Demetrius of Phalerum succeeded those older men, a young man who was indeed the most learned of them all, but trained not so much in arms as in the wrestling-school. And so he delighted the Athenians more than he inflamed them. For he had come forth into the sun and dust not as if from a military tent, but as if from the shady retreats of Theophrastus, a most learned man.
passages.notes: 'Proces serat' is a scanning split of 'processerat'. 'phalereus' at the opening refers to Demetrius of Phalerum.

passages.original: hic primus inflexit orationem et eam mollem teneramque reddidit et suavis, sicut fuit, videri maluit quam gravis; sed suavitate ea, qua perfunderet animos, non qua perfringeret, [et] tantum ut memoriam concinnitatis suae, non, quem ad modum de Pericle scripsit Eupolis, cum delectatione aculeos etiam relinqueret in animis eorum a quibus esset auditus.
passages.english: He was the first to bend oratory and make it soft and tender, and he preferred to seem charming, as he was, rather than weighty; but with a charm that would suffuse minds, not break through them, so that he left only the memory of his elegance, and not, as Eupolis wrote of Pericles, stings as well as delight in the minds of those by whom he had been heard.
passages.notes: The bracketed [et] is deleted by the editor and is not translated.

passages.original: itaque ait Aristoteles, cum sublatis in Sicilia tyrannis res privatae longo intervallo iudiciis repeterentur, tum primum, quod esset acuta illa gens et controversia †natura, artem et praecepta Siculos Coracem et Tisiam conscripsisse—nam antea neminem solitum via nec arte, sed accurate tamen et descripte plerosque dicere—;
passages.english: And so Aristotle says that when, after the tyrants had been removed in Sicily, private property was being reclaimed through the courts after a long interval, then for the first time, because that people was sharp-witted and by nature given to dispute, the Sicilians Corax and Tisias wrote down an art and precepts [of speaking]. For before that, no one had been accustomed to speak by method or art, though most spoke carefully and in an orderly way;
passages.notes: The obelus marks a corrupt word before 'natura'. 'Given to dispute' translates the sense the context seems to require.

passages.original: quod idem fecisse Gorgiam, quem singularum rerum laudes vituperationesque conscripsisse, quod iudicaret hoc oratoris esse maxime proprium, rem augere posse laudando vituperandoque rursus affligere; huic Antiphontem Rhamnusium similia quaedam habuisse conscripta; quo neminem umquam melius ullam oravisse capitis causam, cum se ipse defenderet, [se audiente] locuples auctor scripsit Thucydides;
passages.english: and that Gorgias had done the same, writing praises and censures of particular things, because he judged that this was most especially proper to the orator: to be able to magnify a thing by praising it and, in turn, to cast it down by censuring it; that Antiphon of Rhamnus had written some similar pieces; and that no one ever pleaded any capital case better than he did when he defended himself, as Thucydides, a reliable authority, wrote, [having heard him himself].
passages.notes: '[se audiente]' is bracketed by the edition as doubtful.

passages.original: quis enim aut Argivum oratorem aut Corinthium aut Thebanum scit fuisse temporibus illis? nisi quid de Epaminonda docto homine suspicari libet. Lacedaemonium vero usque ad hoc tempus audivi fuisse neminem. Menelaum ipsum dulcem ilium quidem tradit Homerus, sed pauca dicentem. Brevitas autem laus est interdum in aliqua parte dicendi, in universa eloquentia laudem non habet.
passages.english: For who knows of there having been any orator of Argos, or of Corinth, or of Thebes in those times? Unless one cares to make some guess about Epaminondas, a learned man. And of a Spartan orator, I have heard of none right up to this time. Homer records that Menelaus himself was indeed pleasant, but spoke few words. Brevity, however, is sometimes a merit in some part of speaking; in eloquence as a whole it earns no praise.

passages.original: ut enim hominis decus ingenium, sic ingeni ipsius lumen est eloquentia, qua virum excellentem praeclare tum illi homines florem populi esse dixerunt— Suadaeque medulla.Πειθὼ quam vocant Graeci, cuius effector est orator, hanc Suadam appellavit Ennius [eius autem Cethegum medullam fuisse vult], ut, quam deam in Pericli labris scripsit Eupolis sessitavisse, huius hic medullam nostrum oratorem fuisse dixerit.
passages.english: For as talent is the glory of a man, so eloquence is the light of talent itself, and on account of it the men of that time splendidly called this outstanding man the 'flower of the people' and 'the marrow of Persuasion.' What the Greeks call Peithō, of which the orator is the producer, Ennius called Suada, and he means that Cethegus was its marrow; so that, whereas Eupolis wrote that this goddess sat on the lips of Pericles, Ennius said that our orator was her marrow.
passages.notes: The bracketed clause ('he means that Cethegus was its marrow') is marked by the editor as a probable interpolation. 'Suadaeque medulla' is a quotation from Ennius.

passages.original: et id ipsum nisi unius esset Enni testimonio cognitum, hunc vetustas, ut alios fortasse multos, oblivione obruisset. Illius autem aetatis qui sermo fuerit ex Naevianis scriptis intellegi potest. His enim consulibus, ut in veteribus commentariis scriptum est, Naevius est mortuus; quamquam Varro noster diligentissimus investigator antiquitatis putat in hoc erratum vitamque Naevi producit longius. Nam Plautus P. Claudio L. Porcio viginti annis post illos quos ante dixi consulibus mortuus est, Catone censore.
passages.english: And had even this not been known through the testimony of Ennius alone, time would have buried him in oblivion, as perhaps it has many others. What the language of that age was can be understood from the writings of Naevius. For Naevius died in the consulship of these men, as is written in old records; although our Varro, a most careful investigator of antiquity, thinks there is an error in this and extends Naevius' life further. For Plautus died in the consulship of Publius Claudius and Lucius Porcius, twenty years after the consuls I named before, when Cato was censor.

passages.original: Tuditano consulibus docuit anno ipso ante quam natus est Ennius, post Romam conditam autem quartodecimo et quingentensimo, ut hic ait, quem nos sequimur. Est enim inter scriptores de numero annorum controversia. Accius autem a Q. Maximo quintum consule captum Tarento scripsit Livium annis xxx post quam eum fabulam docuisse et Atticus scribit et nos in antiquis commentariis invenimus,
passages.english: [...] in the consulship of [Gaius Claudius, son of Caecus, and Marcus] Tuditanus, [Livius] produced [a play] in the very year before Ennius was born, and in the five hundred and fourteenth year after the founding of Rome, as the author whom we follow says. For there is disagreement among writers about the count of years. Accius, however, wrote that Livius was captured at Tarentum by Quintus Maximus in his fifth consulship, thirty years after he had produced a play, as both Atticus writes and we have found in old records,
passages.notes: The sentence begins in the preceding context. Cicero's point is that Accius dates Livius wrongly; the relative clause 'post quam... invenimus' is compressed.

passages.original: quorum Gai filius, qui consul cum Domitio fuit, unam orationem de sociis et nomine Latino contra C. Gracchum reliquit sane et bonam et nobilem. Tum Atticus: Quid ergo? estne ista Fanni? nam varia opinio pueris nobis erat. Alii a C. Persio litterato homine scriptam esse aiebant, illo quem significat valde doctum esse Lucilius; alii multos nobilis, quod quisque potuisset, in illam orationem contulisse.
passages.english: Of these, the son of Gaius, who was consul with Domitius, left a single speech, On the Allies and the Latin Name, against Gaius Gracchus, a really good and distinguished one. Then Atticus said: 'What then? Is it really by Fannius? For when we were boys opinion was divided. Some said it was written by Gaius Persius, a man of letters, the one whom Lucilius indicates as very learned; others said that many nobles had contributed to that speech whatever each could.'

passages.original: Nihil enim tam dissimile quam Cotta Sulpicio, et uterque aequalibus suis plurimum praestitit. Qua re hoc doctoris intellegentis est videre, quo ferat natura sua quemque, et ea duce utentem sic instituere, ut Isocratem in acerrimo ingenio Theopompi et lenissimo Ephori dixisse traditum est, alteri se calcaria adhibere alteri frenos.
passages.english: For nothing is so unlike as Cotta is to Sulpicius, and yet each greatly surpassed his contemporaries. Therefore it is the task of an intelligent teacher to see where each person's nature carries him, and, using that as his guide, to train him accordingly, just as Isocrates is reported to have said, regarding the very fiery talent of Theopompus and the very mild one of Ephorus, that to the one he applied spurs, to the other reins.

passages.original: hoc autem loco voluimus aetatem eius in disparem oratorum aetatem includere. Quamquam id quidem omnibus usu venire necesse fuit, quibus paulo longior vita contigit, ut et cum multo maioribus natu quam essent ipsi et cum aliquanto minoribus compararentur. Vt Accius isdem aedilibus ait se et Pacuvium docuisse fabulam, cum ille octoginta, ipse triginta annos natus esset:
passages.english: But at this point we wanted to fit his lifetime into the differing lifetimes of the orators. Yet this necessarily happens to all who are granted a somewhat longer life: they are compared both with men much older than themselves and with men considerably younger. So Accius says that he and Pacuvius put on a play under the same aediles, when Pacuvius was eighty and he himself thirty years old:

passages.original: Nihil tam tenerum quam illius comprensio verborum, nihil tam flexibile, nihil quod magis ipsius arbitrio fingeretur, ut nullius oratoris aeque in potestate fuerit: quae primum ita pura erat ut nihil liquidius, ta libere fluebat ut nusquam adhaeresceret; nullum nisi loco positum et tamquam in vermiculato emblemate, ut ait Lucilius, structum verbum videres; nec vero ullum aut durum aut insolens aut humile aut [in] longius ductum; ac non propria verba rerum sed pleraque translata, sic tamen ut ea non inruisse in alienum locum sed immigrasse in suum diceres;
passages.english: Nothing was so delicate as his arrangement of words, nothing so pliant, nothing more shaped at his own will, so that it was in no orator's power to the same degree: it was, first, so pure that nothing was clearer, and it flowed so freely that it nowhere stuck; you would see no word not set in its place and fitted, as Lucilius says, as in an inlaid mosaic; nor indeed any word harsh, or unusual, or low, or drawn out too far; and not the proper words for things, but most of them metaphorical, yet in such a way that you would say they had not burst into another's place but had moved into their own;
passages.notes: 'ta' read as 'tam' (scanning error). The bracketed [in] is deleted by the editor.

passages.original: si omnis: qui potes, cum sint ipsi dissimillimi inter se? In quo illud etiam quaero, Phalereus ille Demetrius Atticene dixerit. Mihi quidem ex illius orationibus redolere ipsae Athenae videntur. At est floridior, ut ita dicam, quam Hyperides, quam Lysias: natura quaedam aut voluntas ita dicendi fuit.
passages.english: If all of them, how can you, when they are themselves most unlike one another? On this point I also ask whether the famous Demetrius of Phalerum spoke in the Attic manner. To me, at least, Athens itself seems to breathe from his speeches. Yet he is more florid, so to speak, than Hyperides, than Lysias: it was a certain natural bent, or a choice, to speak that way.

passages.original: et quidem duo fuerunt per idem tempus dissimiles inter se, sed Attici tamen; quorum Charisius multarum orationum, quas scribebat aliis, cum cupere videretur imitari Lysiam; Demochares autem, qui fuit Demostheni sororis filius, et orationes scripsit aliquot et earum rerum historiam quae erant Athenis ipsius aetate gestae non tam historico quam oratorio genere perscripsit. Atque Charisi vult Hegesias esse similis, isque se ita putat Atticum, ut veros illos prae se paene agrestis putet.
passages.english: And indeed there were two men in the same period who were unlike each other, but Attic nonetheless: of these, Charisius [was the author] of many speeches, which he wrote for others, since he seemed eager to imitate Lysias; Demochares, who was the son of Demosthenes' sister, both wrote a number of speeches and composed a history of the events that took place at Athens in his own lifetime, in a manner not so much historical as oratorical. And Hegesias wants to be like Charisius, and he considers himself so Attic that he regards those true [Attic orators] as almost rustic compared with himself.

passages.original: risus cum velit, cum velit fletus: ut qui haec procul videat, etiam si quid agatur nesciat, at placere tamen et in scaena esse Roscium intellegat. Haec cui contingant, eum scito Attice dicere, ut de Pericle audimus, ut de Hyperide, ut de Aeschine, de ipso quidem Demosthene maxime.
passages.english: laughter when he wishes, tears when he wishes: so that someone seeing this from a distance, even if he does not know what is being pleaded, may still understand that [the speaker] is pleasing and that a Roscius is on the stage. Whoever achieves this, know that he speaks in the Attic manner, as we hear of Pericles, of Hyperides, of Aeschines, and most of all, indeed, of Demosthenes himself.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence; the verb governing 'risus... fletus' (presumably 'he moves/stirs') lies in the preceding text.

passages.original: Tum Atticus: Aliquotiens sum, inquit, conatus, sed interpellare nolui. Nunc quoniam iam ad perorandum spectare videtur sermo tuus, dicam, opinor, quod sentio. Tu vero, inquam, Tite. Tum ille: Ego, inquit, ironiam illam quam in Socrate dicunt fuisse, qua ille in Platonis et Xenophontis et Aeschini libris utitur, facetam et elegantem puto. Est enim et minime inepti hominis et eiusdem etiam faceti, cum de sapientia disceptetur, hanc sibi ipsum detrahere, eis tribuere inludentem, qui eam sibi adrogant, ut apud Platonem Socrates in caelum effert laudibus Protagoram Hippiam Prodicum Gorgiam ceteros, se autem omnium rerum inscium fingit et rudem. Decet hoc nescio quo modo ilium, nec Epicuro, qui id reprehendit, assentior.
passages.english: Then Atticus said: 'Several times I have tried, but I did not want to interrupt. Now, since your discourse already seems to be heading for its conclusion, I will, I think, say what I feel.' 'Do, Titus,' I said. Then he said: 'I think that irony which they say was in Socrates, which he uses in the books of Plato, Xenophon and Aeschines, witty and elegant. For it is the mark of a man by no means foolish, and also witty, when wisdom is being debated, to deny it to himself and, mockingly, to attribute it to those who claim it for themselves; as in Plato Socrates praises Protagoras, Hippias, Prodicus, Gorgias and the rest to the skies, but pretends that he himself is ignorant of everything and untaught. This somehow suits him, and I do not agree with Epicurus, who censures it.'
